title: SEAMLESS Survey: A Closer Look at Seven Local Volume Dwarf Galaxies in Diverse Environments
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to AAS Journals. Comments are welcome
summary: We present Hubble Space Telescope (HST) imaging of six Local Volume dwarf galaxies identified by the SEAMLESS survey - Cetus B, Hydrus A, Ursa Major C, Hydra B, Grapes, and M83-dw14 - along with Centaurus C (Cen C), discovered serendipitously in the M83-dw14 field. We report the discovery of M83-dw14 and Cen C for the first time. Our HST imaging resolves each system into individual stars, enabling measurements of tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) distances (3.6-6.5 Mpc), structural parameters, and star formation histories (SFHs). We complement these data with new HI observations from the Very Large Array for Ursa Major C, Hydra B, and M83-dw14 (also covering Cen C), and from the Green Bank Telescope for Grapes, together with existing HI limits for Cetus B and Hydrus A. With accurate TRGB distances, we place each target in its environmental context, ranging from a confirmed satellite (M83-dw14) to isolated systems (Hydrus A, Hydra B, Grapes, Cen C). Cen C ($M_V=-7.96$) is among the faintest isolated dwarfs known. It matches the size and luminosity of Leo T, the lowest mass gas-rich galaxy currently known, yet unlike Leo T it shows neither detected HI ($\log(M_{\rm HI}/M_{\odot})<5.3$) nor recent star formation. Ursa Major C shows strongly asymmetric, spatially offset HI, suggesting that feedback may efficiently displace gas in such low-mass systems. Overall, our sample exhibits a broad range of SFHs and quenching states that does not track simply with present-day environment. This diversity is consistent with recent evidence that similarly varied SFHs occur even among isolated low-mass dwarfs, pointing to the important roles of inhomogeneous reionization, stochastic mass assembly, and internal feedback alongside environmental effects.

AI.tldr: HST imaging of seven Local Volume dwarf galaxies yields TRGB distances, structures, and star formation histories, revealing a diversity of quenching states that does not simply track environment.
AI.motivation: The SEAMLESS survey identified several nearby dwarf galaxies, several of which were poorly resolved or unconfirmed, and the drivers of their gas content, star formation, and quenching states relative to their environment remain unclear.
AI.method: Resolved HST imaging of Cetus B, Hydrus A, Ursa Major C, Hydra B, Grapes, M83-dw14, and newly discovered Cen C to measure TRGB distances, structural parameters, and SFHs; combined with VLA HI observations (Ursa Major C, Hydra B, M83-dw14, Cen C), GBT data for Grapes, and existing HI limits.
AI.result: TRGB distances of 3.6-6.5 Mpc place targets from confirmed satellite (M83-dw14) to isolated systems. Cen C (M_V=-7.96) is among the faintest isolated dwarfs, matching Leo T in size and luminosity but lacking HI (log(M_HI/M_sun)<5.3) and recent star formation. Ursa Major C shows asymmetric, spatially offset HI, suggesting feedback displaces gas efficiently. The sample shows broad diversity in SFHs and quenching states not tracking present-day environment.
AI.conclusion: The varied SFHs and quenching states are consistent with additional roles of inhomogeneous reionization, stochastic mass assembly, and internal feedback alongside environmental effects, even among isolated low-mass dwarfs.

title: Chaos and loss: reevaluating the loss-cone formalism in the context of chaotic diving orbits in flattened potentials
comment: 23 pages, 1 appendix
summary: The region close to a massive black hole is one of the few truly spherical geometries in galactic dynamics. Stellar structures, which dominate from pc to kpc scales, are generally at least flattened (axisymmetric) if not more irregular and time evolving. Here we show that orbits that pass between these diverse geometries are commonly chaotic, especially those which dive - visiting their minimum possible periapse. We show that these chaotic diving orbits are common across a wide range of potentials, and can lead to large variation in angular momentum orbit to orbit. We characterise the transition from regular to chaotic orbits with a notional critical angular momentum, $j_d$. We then model the flux of orbits into the loss cone including the effects of these diving orbits combined with evolution through two-body scattering. Systems which cross into the chaotic region are quickly advected away, and thus there is a large net flux across the boundary. We formulate the problem as a probability density, rather than a number density, allowing us to find a true equilibrium state. We find that the rate of disruptions when including diving orbits is boosted by a multiplicative factor of $1+\ln(j_d/j_t)$, where $j_t$ is the angular momentum corresponding to a disruption. This boost can increase disruption rates by an order of magnitude compared to the classical loss cone formalism.

AI.tldr: Orbits passing between the near-spherical region around a massive black hole and the flattened stellar structures farther out are commonly chaotic "diving" orbits; accounting for them boosts tidal disruption rates by a factor 1+ln(j_d/j_t), potentially an order of magnitude above the classical loss-cone formalism.
AI.motivation: The near-BH region is one of the few truly spherical geometries in galactic dynamics, while the stellar structures dominating pc-to-kpc scales are flattened or irregular. The transition between these geometries, and the resulting orbital chaos, is not accounted for in classical loss-cone treatments of stellar flux into the disruption region.
AI.method: The authors identify and characterize chaotic orbits that dive to their minimum periapse across a wide range of potentials, defining a critical angular momentum j_d marking the regular-to-chaotic transition. They then model the flux of orbits into the loss cone, combining the effect of these diving orbits with two-body scattering evolution, and reformulate the problem in terms of a probability density (rather than a number density) to obtain a true equilibrium state.
AI.result: Diving orbits are common across a wide range of potentials, exhibit large orbit-to-orbit angular momentum variation, and systems crossing into the chaotic region are rapidly advected away, producing a large net flux across the boundary. Including diving orbits multiplies the disruption rate by 1+ln(j_d/j_t), where j_t is the angular momentum for disruption — a boost of up to an order of magnitude over the classical loss-cone result.
AI.conclusion: Chaotic diving orbits connecting the spherical near-BH region to the flattened outer stellar structure provide a significant additional channel for loss-cone feeding, and the classical loss-cone formalism substantially underestimates disruption rates when this effect is neglected.

title: Bridging Scales: Multi-Zone GRMHD-Informed Anisotropic AGN Feedback in Galaxies
comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables
summary: We present a galaxy-scale black hole (BH) accretion and feedback model incorporating results from multi-zone general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations spanning the event horizon to the Bondi radius. The model replaces a fixed suppression of the Bondi rate with a nuclear-environment-dependent factor, $κ^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$, set by the local ratio of Bondi to gravitational radius, and distributes outflow mass, kinetic energy, and thermal energy according to the angular structure measured in the large-dynamic-range GRMHD calculations. We apply it to idealized isolated simulations of an M87*-like massive elliptical and a Milky Way/Sgr A*-like galaxy, spanning over three orders of magnitude in BH mass without tuning accretion or feedback efficiencies to match observables. In the M87*-like system, the GRMHD-informed angle-dependent feedback model suppresses late-time stellar mass growth more effectively than the isotropic reference model, despite similar long-term BH accretion rates. Varying the uncertain mass loading of the collimated polar component has a modest impact on BH growth and star formation, indicating that feedback anisotropy matters more than its detailed mass loading. We find that $κ^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$ varies with nuclear environment and time, yielding BH growth histories markedly different from fixed-suppression models. For Sgr A*, this variable factor yields an accretion rate more consistent with Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) constraints than a fixed, suppressed Bondi model. These results show that nuclear-environment-dependent accretion and feedback angular structure affect BH-galaxy evolution, requiring subgrid models to include more than a universal Bondi suppression factor and a scalar feedback efficiency.

AI.tldr: A galaxy-scale BH accretion/feedback model using multi-zone GRMHD results, with environment-dependent Bondi suppression and angle-dependent outflows, reproduces EHT-consistent Sgr A* accretion and shows feedback anisotropy shapes BH-galaxy evolution.
AI.motivation: Standard subgrid models use a fixed Bondi suppression factor and scalar feedback efficiency, ignoring how accretion and outflows depend on nuclear environment and angular structure. The authors aim to replace these simplifications with GRMHD-informed, environment-dependent prescriptions.
AI.method: They build a model spanning horizon to Bondi radius based on multi-zone GRMHD simulations. The Bondi rate is multiplied by a factor κ^hot_cho set by the local ratio of Bondi to gravitational radius. Outflow mass, kinetic energy, and thermal energy are distributed per the angular structure measured in large-dynamic-range GRMHD runs. The model is applied to idealized isolated simulations of an M87*-like massive elliptical and a Sgr A*-like galaxy, spanning >3 orders of magnitude in BH mass, without tuning accretion or feedback efficiencies.
AI.result: For the M87*-like system, the angle-dependent feedback suppresses late-time stellar mass growth more effectively than an isotropic reference at similar long-term BH accretion rates. Varying the polar-component mass loading has modest impact on BH growth and star formation, so anisotropy matters more than mass loading. κ^hot_cho varies with nuclear environment and time, producing BH growth histories distinct from fixed-suppression models. For Sgr A*, the variable factor yields an accretion rate more consistent with EHT constraints than a fixed suppressed Bondi model.
AI.conclusion: Nuclear-environment-dependent accretion and feedback angular structure affect BH-galaxy co-evolution. Subgrid models need more than a universal Bondi suppression factor and a scalar feedback efficiency.

title: How to feed your dragon: the role of turbulence in AGN activity
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, accepted in ApJ
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are thought to be important drivers of galaxy evolution. However, the way AGN jets couple their energy to the interstellar medium (ISM) remains poorly understood. Recent observations have revealed $\sim$kpc-scale jets in galaxies of different morphological types. Here, we use idealized turbulent box simulations with accreting black holes to investigate how jet-ISM interactions and feedback shape the evolution of jets. We show that a turbulent ISM is a key ingredient in both jet launching and jet propagation. Without turbulence, jet feedback initially shuts off the cold gas supply to the black hole and the system enters a steady state with jet power $\leq 10^{39}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ for a $10^{6}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ black hole. In a turbulent medium, jets fill voids with hot diffuse material which the turbulence then carries away, replenishing the black hole's fuel supply. However, above a critical jet efficiency factor, the jet begins to significantly deplete its fuel supply and enters a self-limiting accretion regime. This critical factor depends on the ISM Mach number, with lower turbulence yielding a lower threshold. Moreover, while the jet power depends on the ambient gas density in the vicinity of the black hole, we find that, at fixed turbulent structure, the morphology and extent of jet propagation are largely insensitive to the average background density; turbulence in the ISM dominates over mean density in setting how far jets propagate, although denser media experience higher total energy injection and stronger heating.

AI.tldr: Idealized turbulent box simulations with accreting black holes show that a turbulent ISM is essential for both jet launching and propagation, and that jets transition to a self-limiting accretion regime above a critical efficiency factor that depends on the ISM Mach number.
AI.motivation: AGN jets are important drivers of galaxy evolution, but how they couple their energy to the interstellar medium (ISM) is poorly understood. Recent observations reveal kpc-scale jets across morphological types, motivating a controlled study of jet-ISM interaction and feedback.
AI.method: Idealized turbulent box simulations with accreting black holes, varying ISM turbulence (Mach number) and mean background density, to study jet launching, propagation, and feedback.
AI.result: Without turbulence, jet feedback shuts off the cold gas supply and the system reaches a steady state with jet power <=1e39 erg/s for a 1e6 Msun black hole. With turbulence, jets fill voids with hot diffuse material that turbulence carries away, replenishing the fuel supply; above a critical jet efficiency factor the jet depletes its fuel and enters a self-limiting accretion regime. This threshold decreases with lower turbulence (lower Mach number). At fixed turbulent structure, jet morphology and extent are largely insensitive to mean background density; turbulence dominates over mean density in setting propagation distance, though denser media yield higher total energy injection and stronger heating.
AI.conclusion: Turbulence is a key ingredient in jet launching and propagation; it regulates black hole fueling and sets a Mach-dependent critical efficiency for self-limiting feedback. Jet propagation distance is governed primarily by turbulence rather than mean density, while denser environments produce stronger heating.

title: Likely Metal Scarring in the Magnetic White Dwarf LHS 2534
comment: 4 pages, 1 figure, Published in RNAAS
summary: There are only three white dwarfs known to possess metal-enriched polar caps due to magnetically guided accretion. These rare systems offer a unique opportunity to study planetesimal accretion and how magnetic fields influence the spreading of material across the atmosphere. To better study these processes however, more targets are needed. Here we report our findings from an observing campaign on the magnetic white dwarf LHS 2534. Time-resolved spectra at the MMT show clear variability in the strength of the Na I and Cr I features. We find that the strengths of these features vary over a period of 19.46 and 19.36 hours respectively, closely matching the 20.22 hour period determined from K2 photometry. Our findings demonstrate the ability to detect and study these variable objects with spectroscopy, and time-series observations of similar targets in the future will provide more insight into how these atmospheres form.

AI.tldr: Time-resolved MMT spectroscopy of the magnetic white dwarf LHS 2534 reveals rotationally modulated Na I and Cr I features, confirming it as a metal-enriched polar cap accretor.
AI.motivation: Only three white dwarfs are known to host metal-enriched polar caps from magnetically guided accretion, limiting study of planetesimal accretion and magnetic-field-driven atmospheric spreading; more targets are needed.
AI.method: Time-resolved spectra of the magnetic white dwarf LHS 2534 obtained at the MMT, measuring variability in Na I and Cr I line strengths and comparing periods with K2 photometry.
AI.result: Na I and Cr I feature strengths vary with periods of 19.46 and 19.36 hours, closely matching the 20.22-hour period from K2 photometry.
AI.conclusion: Spectroscopy can detect and characterize these variable polar-cap systems; future time-series observations of similar targets will clarify how these unusual atmospheres form.

title: Learning Galaxy Kinematics from Spatially Unresolved Spectra
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures
summary: Galaxy kinematics encode information about the assembly histories of galaxies and the black holes at their centers, motivating the measurement of kinematic parameters for large galaxy populations. In particular, such parameters have been shown to help identify galaxies that host supermassive black hole binaries, a major outstanding question in multi-messenger astrophysics. Yet, inferring kinematic properties from spatially unresolved observations, where distant galaxies appear as point sources, remains a challenge. Spectroscopy can address this challenge because Doppler effects encode internal motions into spectral line profiles. Exploiting this encoding requires knowing how spatial structures map onto the line profiles but this cannot be derived from first principles for complex systems such as galaxies. We present a neural network trained on spatially resolved spectra that infers kinematic properties from spatially integrated spectra, offering two advantages over classical approaches: it learns the kinematic encoding directly from data without requiring spatial resolution and remains effective even when spectral resolution only marginally resolves the lines. This enables recovering the kinematic properties for millions of unresolved galaxies in existing and future surveys.

AI.tldr: A neural network trained on spatially resolved spectra infers galaxy kinematic properties from unresolved, spatially integrated spectra, enabling kinematic measurements for millions of distant galaxies.
AI.motivation: Galaxy kinematics trace galaxy assembly and central black hole histories, and can help identify galaxies hosting supermassive black hole binaries—an open question in multi-messenger astrophysics. Measuring these parameters for large populations is therefore desirable, but distant galaxies appear as point sources, and there is no first-principles mapping from spatial structure to integrated line profiles for complex systems.
AI.method: The authors train a neural network on spatially resolved spectra so that it learns the mapping between internal spatial kinematics and spectral line profiles directly from data. The trained model is then applied to spatially integrated (unresolved) spectra to infer kinematic properties.
AI.result: The network learns the kinematic encoding without needing spatial resolution and remains effective even when spectral resolution only marginally resolves the lines, yielding a data-driven alternative to classical approaches.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables recovery of kinematic properties for millions of unresolved galaxies in existing and future surveys.

title: Spectroscopic observations of periodic bursty ejections during a dome-spire-shaped jet
summary:
Context: The study investigates the complexity of the formation and evolution of a dome-spire-shaped jet (or anemone jet) that originated in an active region and was presumably driven by null-point magnetic reconnection.
  Aims: We aim to provide a quantitative estimation of multi-temperature plasma dynamics and physical parameters of the jet and its blob-like features, together with its temporal evolution in three-dimensional perspective.
  Methods: For this, we analyze unique sit-and-stare spectral (Si IV, Mg II k, and C II) and slit-jaw imaging 1400 Å and 2796 Å observations obtained with the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS), with a slit uniquely positioned just above the assumed reconnection site. Co-observations taken with the Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph of the Goode Solar Telescope in the chromospheric H$α$ and Ca II 8542.10 Å lines were also analyzed. These data are complemented by EUV imaging information from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly on board the Solar Dynamics Observatory.
  Results: The IRIS observations reveal that the jet is formed by multiple periodic ($\sim$30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each associated with strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 Å transition-region emission reaching about $-300$ km/s. More importantly, the ejections are grouped into well-defined packets, each lasting approximately 3--5 min. In contrast, only a single Doppler component is observed in the chromospheric Ca II line. Multi-Gaussian decomposition of the Si IV line profiles reveals a highly accelerated plasma, with line-of-sight speed toward the observer increasing linearly from $\sim$30 to 112 km/s over 66 s, corresponding to an acceleration of 1.3 km/s$^2$. The kinetic energy release rate is estimated in the range of $\sim$1.0$\times10^{24}$--1.0$\times10^{25}$ erg\,s$^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: IRIS sit-and-stare spectra plus GTS/SDO imaging reveal a dome-spire jet built from periodic (~30 s) blob ejections grouped into 3–5 min packets, with strongly blueshifted Si IV (~−300 km/s), a linearly accelerating plasma component (~1.3 km/s²), and kinetic energy release rates of ~1e24–1e25 erg/s.
AI.motivation: Dome-spire (anemone) jets driven by null-point magnetic reconnection remain poorly quantified: their multi-temperature plasma dynamics, blob-like substructure, and temporal evolution in three dimensions are not well constrained, so the paper aims to characterize these quantitatively.
AI.method: Unique IRIS sit-and-stare spectroscopy (Si IV, Mg II k, C II) with the slit placed just above the presumed reconnection site, plus 1400 Å and 2796 Å slit-jaw imaging; complementary chromospheric Hα and Ca II 8542.10 Å spectra from the Goode Solar Telescope Fast Imaging Solar Spectrograph; EUV imaging from SDO/AIA; multi-Gaussian decomposition of Si IV profiles to extract Doppler components and accelerations.
AI.result: The jet consists of multiple periodic (~30 s) plasma ejections with blob-like appearance, each tied to strongly blueshifted Si IV 1402.77 Å transition-region emission near −300 km/s. Ejections are organized into well-defined packets lasting ~3–5 min. Chromospheric Ca II shows only a single Doppler component. Multi-Gaussian fitting reveals a highly accelerated plasma whose line-of-sight speed rises linearly from ~30 to 112 km/s over 66 s (≈1.3 km/s²). Kinetic energy release rate is estimated at ~1.0×10^24–1.0×10^25 erg/s.
AI.conclusion: The dome-spire jet is impulsively built from quasi-periodic (~30 s) blob ejections clustered into minute-scale packets, consistent with intermittent null-point reconnection; the plasma is strongly accelerated, with kinetic energy fluxes spanning ~1e24–1e25 erg/s, indicating an energetically significant contribution to coronal heating and mass supply.

title: The assembly of dusty galaxies at $z \geq 4$: grain growth and the evolutionary origin of the dust-to-stellar-mass scatter
comment: 20 pages, 13 figures; submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Understanding dust evolution is essential for interpreting the properties of galaxies across cosmic time. Nearby galaxies have revealed a detailed picture of dust enrichment, but whether the same picture applies in the early Universe remains unclear. Here we explore the origin of interstellar dust in simulated galaxies at $z \sim 5$. Starting from the dust-to-stellar mass relation, we select five simulated star-forming galaxies with $SFR> 1 M_\odot yr^{-1}$ and $ log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 8$. We focus on three low-mass systems with comparable stellar masses ($log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 8.7$) but significantly different dust masses ($log(M_{\rm dust}/M_\odot) \sim 5.1-6.2$), to investigate the origin of the scatter in the relation. Our analysis combines outputs from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulation dustyGadget, a semi-analytical model for stellar dust production, and radiative-transfer post-processing with SKIRT. We confirm that stellar dust production alone reproduces only the low-dust branch of the relation. Grain growth is required to recover both its S-shape and the observed scatter, as established for nearby galaxies. The transition to efficient grain growth occurs at lower metallicity than locally, consistent with the denser interstellar medium of high-redshift systems. Differences in dust content reflect different stages of galaxy assembly. Progressively longer star formation histories lead to greater chemical enrichment and denser ISM, promoting increasingly efficient grain growth. We therefore identify the assembly stage as the key regulator of dust growth at high redshift. Mock observations show that JWST multi-band imaging can reveal the structural diversity of galaxies within the scatter, although the reconstruction of clumpy morphologies may remain incomplete. Their dust continuum emission remains below the sensitivity of current ALMA continuum surveys.

AI.tldr: Dust evolution at z~5 is investigated with dustyGadget hydrodynamical simulations, a semi-analytical stellar-dust model, and SKIRT radiative transfer. Grain growth is needed to reproduce the S-shape and scatter of the dust-to-stellar mass relation, with the assembly stage as the key regulator.
AI.motivation: While nearby galaxies provide a detailed picture of dust enrichment, it is unclear whether this picture holds in the early Universe. The origin of the scatter in the dust-to-stellar mass relation at high redshift, and the physical processes responsible, remain to be identified.
AI.method: Five simulated star-forming galaxies at z~5 from dustyGadget with SFR > 1 Msun/yr and log(M*/Msun) > 8 were selected. Three low-mass systems with log(M*/Msun) ~ 8.7 but widely different dust masses (log(Mdust/Msun) ~ 5.1-6.2) were analyzed, combining hydrodynamical outputs, a semi-analytical stellar dust production model, and SKIRT radiative-transfer post-processing, including mock JWST and ALMA observables.
AI.result: Stellar dust production alone reproduces only the low-dust branch of the relation. Grain growth is required to recover both the S-shape and the observed scatter. The transition to efficient grain growth occurs at lower metallicity than locally, consistent with the denser high-redshift ISM. Dust content differences track different assembly stages: longer star formation histories yield greater chemical enrichment and denser ISM, enhancing grain growth. Mock JWST multi-band imaging can reveal structural diversity within the scatter, though reconstruction of clumpy morphologies may remain incomplete; dust continuum emission lies below current ALMA continuum survey sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The assembly stage is identified as the key regulator of dust growth at high redshift. The nearby-galaxy framework, with grain growth as the dominant channel, extends to z~5 but with a lower metallicity threshold for efficient growth. JWST imaging can probe the structural diversity within the scatter, while current ALMA surveys cannot detect this dust continuum.

title: Relative Influence of Coronal Properties of CME in their Evolution and Geo-effectiveness
summary: Uncertainties in the coronal mass ejection (CME) properties near the Sun remain a major challenge for accurate space weather forecasting. Understanding the sensitivity of CME evolution to the initial parameters is therefore essential for improving the predictions. We investigate the influence of physical CME properties prescribed at 0.1 AU on their subsequent heliospheric propagation and geoeffectiveness at Earth, using the SWASTi framework. We perform a systematically sampled ensemble of 400 global magnetohydrodynamic simulations by varying the initial CME density, speed, magnetic flux and temperature. We quantify the relative influence of these parameters on CME evolution, plasma properties at L1, and the resulting geomagnetic response. The analysis reveals a clear hierarchy of influence: initial speed primarily controls the peak radial velocity and arrival time at L1, magnetic flux controls the magnetic-field strength, and density governs the peak density and magnetopause compression. Primary parameters account for only half the output variance, highlighting the collective influence of other parameters. Density exhibits the broadest influence across the analyzed outputs. We find a mean arrival-time sensitivities of 2.43h per 100 km/s variation in injection speed and 1.99h per $10^{-18}$ kg/m$^3$ variation in injection density. The CME volume exhibits a two-phase evolution, characterized by an initial gradual expansion followed by a power-law regime with a median expansion index of 2.38. These results establish parameter-specific priorities for CME forecasting, highlighting the importance of constraining CME speed for arrival-time prediction, density for duration and pressure-driven effects, and magnetic flux for geomagnetic response at Earth.

AI.tldr: A 400-member global MHD ensemble shows a clear hierarchy of CME initial-parameter influence: speed governs peak radial velocity and L1 arrival time, magnetic flux governs field strength, and density governs peak density and magnetopause compression, though primary parameters explain only ~half the output variance.
AI.motivation: Uncertainties in near-Sun CME properties hamper space weather forecasting, so understanding how initial CME parameters drive subsequent heliospheric evolution and geoeffectiveness is essential for improving predictions.
AI.method: Systematically sampled ensemble of 400 global MHD simulations using the SWASTi framework, varying initial CME density, speed, magnetic flux and temperature prescribed at 0.1 AU, and quantifying their relative influence on CME evolution, L1 plasma properties and geomagnetic response.
AI.result: Clear hierarchy: initial speed primarily controls peak radial velocity and L1 arrival time, magnetic flux controls magnetic-field strength, and density governs peak density and magnetopause compression. Primary parameters account for only half the output variance; density has the broadest influence. Mean arrival-time sensitivities are 2.43 h per 100 km/s in injection speed and 1.99 h per 1e-18 kg/m^3 in injection density. CME volume shows two-phase evolution—gradual expansion then a power-law regime with median expansion index 2.38.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-specific priorities for CME forecasting are established: constrain CME speed for arrival-time prediction, density for duration and pressure-driven effects, and magnetic flux for geomagnetic response at Earth.

title: Kinematic Decomposition of the BCG and ICL in Abell S1063 and MACS J1206
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: The brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) and the intracluster light (ICL) overlap in space and merge smoothly in surface brightness. Beyond the nearest clusters, measurements of the ICL have therefore relied on photometric definitions. We present a spectral decomposition of the light in cluster cores into BCG and ICL, using deep VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy of Abell S1063 (z=0.35) and MACS J1206.2$-$0847 (z=0.44). Spectral templates of the two components are derived iteratively from the BCG center and the ICL-dominated outskirts, and their weighted sum is fitted to the spectrum of every spatial bin. This enables us to measure the kinematics and the light of the BCG and ICL separately without assuming a boundary or a functional form for their light profiles. The velocity dispersions of the BCG and ICL are $316\pm5$ and $753\pm25\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$, respectively, in AS1063, whereas we obtain $313\pm5$ and $695^{+47}_{-45}\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$ in MACS1206. The ICL is blueshifted relative to the BCG by $75\pm22$ and $148\pm38\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$, respectively, and is ~0.7 dex more metal-poor, at a combined statistical significance of ~$2σ$. Defining the ICL as the light fainter than $μ_{B}=25\ \mathrm{mag\ arcsec^{-2}}$ assigns two-thirds to three-quarters of the kinematically defined ICL to the BCG, while a double Sersic model fits the total profiles well but leaves the division between the two components poorly constrained given the depth and resolution of the current MUSE data. Our kinematic decomposition provides a direct, physically motivated reference for photometric definitions of the ICL.

AI.tldr: A spectral decomposition of cluster core light into BCG and ICL components using VLT/MUSE IFU spectroscopy of Abell S1063 and MACS J1206 separates their kinematics and stellar populations without assuming any boundary or profile form.
AI.motivation: BCG and ICL overlap spatially and merge smoothly in surface brightness, so beyond nearby clusters ICL measurements rely on arbitrary photometric definitions. A physically motivated, boundary-free separation is needed to provide a reference for those photometric definitions.
AI.method: Deep VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy of Abell S1063 (z=0.35) and MACS J1206.2-0847 (z=0.44). Spectral templates for BCG and ICL are derived iteratively from the BCG center and ICL-dominated outskirts; their weighted sum is fitted to every spatial bin spectrum, yielding separate kinematics and light for each component.
AI.result: Velocity dispersions: BCG 316±5 and ICL 753±25 km/s (AS1063); BCG 313±5 and ICL 695(+47/-45) km/s (MACS1206). ICL is blueshifted relative to the BCG by 75±22 and 148±38 km/s, and ~0.7 dex more metal-poor (combined ~2σ). A μ_B=25 mag/arcsec² cut assigns two-thirds to three-quarters of the kinematic ICL to the BCG; a double Sersic fit works well but poorly constrains the division given MUSE depth/resolution.
AI.conclusion: The kinematic decomposition offers a direct, physically motivated benchmark for photometric ICL definitions, showing that surface-brightness thresholds substantially misassign kinematically identified ICL to the BCG.

title: Identifying a High-confidence Candidate of Stellar Coronal Mass Ejection on an M~dwarf
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures and 2 tables. To be published in ApJL
summary: Although coronal mass ejections (CMEs) potentially play an important role in shaping the habitability of exoplanets, the firm detection of flaring-associated CMEs on remote stars remains a challenge task at current stage. We here report time-resolved spectroscopic follow-up observations of a superflare (GWAC~251130A) on an M-dwarf, triggered by the SVOM/GWAC high-cadence transient survey. With an amplitude of $\approx2.5$~mag in $R-$band, the bolometric flaring energy is estimated to be $1.2^{+1.0}_{-0.5}\times10^{35}$~erg. The spectroscopy reveals complex flare-associated plasma motions. A stellar CME candidate on the M-dwarf can be identified on the M~dwarf at high confidence, based on its maximum projected velocity ($V_{\mathrm{max}}\sim1500\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$) measured from the blueshifted broad H$α$ emission line-the second highest among all reported stellar CME candidates. This velocity makes GWAC~251130A one of the only two events with a $V_\mathrm{max}$ exceeding twice the surface escape velocity. Both chromospheric evaporation and condensation can be additionally identified in the flare after the broad-line emission fades away. The CME mass and corresponding kinetic energy along the line-of-sight are estimated to be $\sim3.2\times10^{19}$~g and $\sim2.1\times10^{32}$~erg, respectively, which reinforces the slightly larger expelled mass with depressed kinetic energy in stellar CME than in the solar flare-CME events.

AI.tldr: Time-resolved spectroscopy of the M-dwarf superflare GWAC~251130A reveals a high-confidence stellar CME candidate with a projected velocity of ~1500 km/s, plus chromospheric evaporation and condensation signatures after the flare.
AI.motivation: CMEs may strongly influence exoplanet habitability, yet firm detection of flaring-associated CMEs on remote stars remains challenging.
AI.method: Triggered by the SVOM/GWAC high-cadence transient survey, the authors performed time-resolved spectroscopic follow-up of a superflare on an M-dwarf, analyzing the blueshifted broad H-alpha emission line, plasma motions, and post-flare chromospheric evaporation/condensation; they derived bolometric flare energy and CME mass/kinetic energy.
AI.result: Flare amplitude ~2.5 mag in R-band with bolometric energy 1.2^{+1.0}_{-0.5}×10^35 erg; a high-confidence CME candidate with V_max ~1500 km/s (second highest among stellar CME candidates, and only the second event exceeding twice the surface escape velocity); CME mass ~3.2×10^19 g and line-of-sight kinetic energy ~2.1×10^32 erg; chromospheric evaporation and condensation detected after the broad line fades.
AI.conclusion: GWAC~251130A provides a high-confidence stellar CME candidate, reinforcing that stellar CMEs tend to eject slightly larger masses with depressed kinetic energy compared to solar flare-CME events.

title: NGDEEP: Anchoring the $0.5 < z < 3.5$ Star-Forming Main Sequence at Low Stellar Masses with Ultradeep JWST/NIRISS WFSS
comment: Submitted for publication in ApJL
summary: Here we present deep JWST/NIRISS wide-field slitless spectroscopy (WFSS) that covers $\mathrm{Hα}$ and $\mathrm{Hβ}$ for galaxies at $0.5 < z < 3.5$ in the NGDEEP survey. The NGDEEP NIRISS observations detect emission line fluxes from galaxies in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field to $\mathrm{m_{F150W}} \lesssim$ 28 mag, enabling studies of star-formation based on $\mathrm{Hα}$ (or $\mathrm{Hβ}$, if necessary) in low-mass galaxies with $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) \gtrsim 7}$ at z = 0.5 and $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) \gtrsim 8}$ at z = 3.5. For 284 NGDEEP galaxies with $>3σ$ detections of $\mathrm{Hα}$ or $\mathrm{Hβ}$, we determine dust-corrected star-formation rates, $\mathrm{SFR_{Hα}}$, via flux measurements of these Balmer lines and compare them to the galaxies' stellar masses to investigate the properties of the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) on short, $\sim10$~Myr timescales across three redshift bins. When we contrast the intrinsic scatter in the $\mathrm{Hα}$--based SFMS to that of a SFMS comprised of UV--based SFRs, which trace star formation within the past $\sim 100$~Myr, we find that the \Ha--based SFMS's intrinsic scatter ($\approx0.35-0.5$~dex over $0.5 < z < 3.5$) is $\approx0.2-0.4$~dex higher than the UV--based SFMS's intrinsic scatter at $z < 2.5$. We argue that brief ($\lesssim10$~Myr) bursts of star formation likely account for this disparity in SFMS scatter. Theoretical predictions from the FIRE simulations underestimate the scatter we observe in the $\mathrm{Hα}$--based SFMS at $1.5 < z < 2.5$ and $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) < 9}$ by up to $\approx0.25$~dex, which suggests that low-mass galaxies have burstier star-formation histories than expected on $\lesssim10$~Myr timescales.

AI.tldr: Deep JWST/NIRISS WFSS Hα and Hβ spectroscopy of 284 galaxies at 0.5<z<3.5 in NGDEEP yields SFRs on ~10 Myr timescales; the Hα-based star-forming main sequence shows larger intrinsic scatter (~0.35–0.5 dex) than the UV-based one by ~0.2–0.4 dex at z<2.5, attributed to brief (<10 Myr) starbursts, and exceeds FIRE predictions for low-mass galaxies.
AI.motivation: SFR indicators probe different timescales: Hα traces ~10 Myr and UV traces ~100 Myr, so comparing their main-sequence scatter constrains the burstiness of star-formation histories, especially for low-mass galaxies that remain poorly characterized at high redshift.
AI.method: Wide-field slitless spectroscopy with JWST/NIRISS in the NGDEEP survey covering Hα and Hβ for galaxies at 0.5<z<3.5, reaching m_F150W ≲ 28 mag and probing down to log(M*/M☉)≳7–8. For 284 galaxies with >3σ Balmer-line detections, dust-corrected SFR_Hα is derived from the line fluxes and compared with stellar masses to measure the SFMS and its intrinsic scatter in three redshift bins, benchmarked against UV-based SFRs and FIRE simulations.
AI.result: The Hα-based SFMS has intrinsic scatter of ≈0.35–0.5 dex over 0.5<z<3.5, roughly 0.2–0.4 dex larger than the UV-based SFMS at z<2.5. FIRE simulations underpredict the observed Hα scatter by up to ≈0.25 dex at 1.5<z<2.5 for log(M*/M☉)<9.
AI.conclusion: Short (≲10 Myr) bursts of star formation likely drive the excess scatter in the Hα-based SFMS, indicating that low-mass galaxies have burstier star-formation histories on ≲10 Myr timescales than FIRE predicts.

title: Inferring dominant acceleration mechanisms using the longitudinal spread of solar particle intensities: 28 May 2021 event
summary: Solar energetic particles (SEPs) are typically accelerated during solar eruptions and propagate along magnetic field lines in the inner heliosphere. These eruptions include shock waves driven by coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and magnetic reconnection in solar flares. Disentangling these source mechanisms within the measurements has been a long-standing problem for space physics researchers. Since spacecraft rarely reach the acceleration regions close to the Sun, measured SEP intensities reflect a combination of particle acceleration and interplanetary transport. The method used in this study attempts to identify which of the two main acceleration processes is more dominant for specific particle energies and species in a standalone event. Through this approach, we aim to better identify the signatures associated with these two acceleration phenomena and recognize similar behaviors in measurements with transport effects. This study characterizes the longitudinal spread of the SEP event on 28 May 2021 by fitting Gaussian curves at regular time intervals to particle intensities as a function of spacecraft position. This evolution offers unprecedented detail compared to earlier peak-focused studies, which were also limited to only three observers, while we now benefit from a novel fleet. To support the interpretation of the evolving profiles, we use a 2D SEP transport model to test if the evolution of the SEP distribution can also be caused by interplanetary effects. For this event, we find that the particle distribution of 0.1 MeV electrons remains static, while for 14 and 32 MeV protons, the distribution grows and moves to the west. We suggest that the CME-driven shock is the dominant source for protons, and that the flare is the dominant source only for the studied 0.1 MeV electrons. Interplanetary transport processes could also be contributing to the moving particle distributions.

AI.tldr: By Gaussian-fitting SEP intensities vs. spacecraft longitude at regular time intervals during the 28 May 2021 event and testing against a 2D transport model, the study attributes the westward-growing, propagating proton distributions (14, 32 MeV) to a CME-driven shock source, while the static 0.1 MeV electron distribution is attributed to flare-dominated acceleration.
AI.motivation: SEPs are accelerated by both CME-driven shocks and flare reconnection, and spacecraft rarely sample the near-Sun acceleration regions, so measured intensities mix acceleration and interplanetary transport—making source attribution a long-standing problem. Prior peak-focused studies were also limited to only three observers.
AI.method: Characterize the longitudinal spread of the 28 May 2021 SEP event by fitting Gaussian curves at regular time intervals to particle intensities as a function of spacecraft position, using a novel multi-spacecraft fleet. A 2D SEP transport model is then used to test whether the observed evolution of the distribution could instead be produced by interplanetary effects.
AI.result: The 0.1 MeV electron distribution remains static over time, whereas the 14 and 32 MeV proton distributions grow and shift westward. The time-resolved Gaussian evolution provides far greater detail than earlier peak-based, three-observer analyses.
AI.conclusion: The CME-driven shock is suggested as the dominant source for protons, while the flare dominates only for the studied 0.1 MeV electrons. Interplanetary transport processes may additionally contribute to the moving particle distributions. The approach helps identify signatures of the two acceleration mechanisms and recognize them in transport-affected measurements.

title: The Size-Mass Relation and Inside-Out Quenching of Massive Quiescent Galaxies at $2<z<3$ with JWST PRIMER and MINERVA
comment: 27 pages, 13 figures, Submitted to ApJ, Comments Welcome
summary: We investigate the morphology, size--mass relations, and spatially resolved star formation histories of 26 massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon ($2 < z < 3$) in the Ultra-Deep Survey field using deep JWST NIRCam imaging from the PRIMER and MINERVA surveys. Combining 16 broadband and medium-band filters with empirical point spread function matching, we perform single-Sérsic modeling and bulge--disk decompositions with pysersic across six filters (F115W to F444W), alongside Bayesian size--mass fitting with dynesty. In the rest-frame optical (F200W), the size--mass relation exhibits a steep slope of $α= 0.59 \pm 0.12$ and effective radius of $A = 0.83_{-0.07}^{+0.08}\ \mathrm{kpc}$ at $M_* = 5 \times 10^{10}\ M_\odot$. In the rest-frame near-infrared (F356W), we derive $α= 0.56 \pm 0.13$ and a more compact radius of $A = 0.70_{-0.06}^{+0.07}\ \mathrm{kpc}$. Galaxy sizes shrink by $\approx 22\%$ from F115W to F444W, reflecting negative color gradients and centrally concentrated mass profiles. Two-thirds of the sample are bulge-dominated ($B/T \ge 0.5$), whereas one-third are disk-dominated. Central bulges are ultra-compact ($R_{e,\mathrm{Bulge}} \approx 0.49\ \mathrm{kpc}$) with negligible mass dependence, whereas outer disks extend to $R_{e,\mathrm{Disk}} \approx 1.4\text{--}1.5\ \mathrm{kpc}$. Resolved spectral energy distribution modeling with piXedfit demonstrates positive radial specific star formation rate gradients and inner regions that formed at least $\approx 0.7\ \mathrm{Gyr}$ earlier and quenched faster than their outskirts. These results confirm inside-out quenching, consistent with dissipative gas compaction assembling the dense core, active galactic nucleus feedback halting central star formation, and the compact bulge dynamically stabilizing the surviving disk against fragmentation.

AI.tldr: JWST NIRCam imaging of 26 massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon reveals steep size–mass relations, ~22% size shrinkage toward longer wavelengths, bulge-dominated structures with ultra-compact bulges, and positive radial sSFR gradients indicating inside-out quenching via dissipative compaction and AGN feedback.
AI.motivation: Massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon (2 < z < 3) are poorly characterized in terms of their structural morphology, size–mass scaling, and spatially resolved star formation histories. The authors aim to connect structural properties (bulges/disks) with quenching mechanisms by leveraging deep, multi-band JWST imaging to trace rest-frame optical through near-infrared structure and resolved star formation.
AI.method: Deep JWST NIRCam imaging from PRIMER and MINERVA in the Ultra-Deep Survey field, combining 16 broadband and medium-band filters with empirical PSF matching. Single-Sérsic modeling and bulge–disk decomposition using pysersic across six filters (F115W–F444W), plus Bayesian size–mass fitting with dynesty. Resolved SED modeling with piXedfit to derive radial star formation histories and sSFR profiles.
AI.result: Size–mass relation is steep: α = 0.59 ± 0.12 (F200W, rest-frame optical) with A = 0.83 kpc at M* = 5×10^10 M⊙, and α = 0.56 ± 0.13 with a more compact A = 0.70 kpc in F356W (rest-frame NIR). Sizes shrink ~22% from F115W to F444W (negative color gradients, centrally concentrated mass). Two-thirds are bulge-dominated (B/T ≥ 0.5), one-third disk-dominated. Bulges are ultra-compact (Re,Bulge ≈ 0.49 kpc, negligible mass dependence); disks extend to Re,Disk ≈ 1.4–1.5 kpc. Resolved SEDs show positive radial sSFR gradients; inner regions formed ≥~0.7 Gyr earlier and quenched faster than outskirts.
AI.conclusion: The results confirm inside-out quenching in massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon, consistent with a scenario where dissipative gas compaction assembles a dense central core, AGN feedback halts central star formation, and the compact bulge dynamically stabilizes the surviving disk against fragmentation.

title: Decay of space plasma turbulence downstream of bow shocks: MMS magnetosheath unbiased campaign observations
summary: Turbulence properties in the solar wind change with increasing heliospheric distance. Observations from different missions have shown how spectral indices converge towards a $f^{-5/3}$ spectrum in the inertial range as the solar wind reaches one astronomical unit, and how the cascade rate decays as the plasma moves away from the Sun. We evaluate whether these properties display similar trends in a smaller astrophysical system, that of a planetary magnetosheath. Using data from the 2023 Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) unbiased magnetosheath campaign, we determine the evolution of the spectral indices and the cascade rate along 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings. WIND observations permitted to monitor the state of the solar wind during the campaign and allowed to study the impact of the upstream plasma conditions on the evolution of the cascade rate downstream the bow shock. Our results show an increase of the cascade rate between two to three orders of magnitude after the plasma crosses the bow shock into the magnetosheath. Once in the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing distance to the bow shock in a way similar to solar wind observations, despite the smaller size of the system. Incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates of the cascade rate show a clear power-law decay of the cascade rate in the magnetosheath, particularly for the cases with upstream slow wind. This suggests that the way energy is injected into the system plays a role in the decay of turbulence as the plasma moves away from the bow shock.

AI.tldr: Turbulence in Earth's magnetosheath mirrors solar wind trends: cascade rate jumps 2–3 orders of magnitude across the bow shock, then decays as a power law with distance, modulated by upstream solar wind conditions.
AI.motivation: Solar wind turbulence evolves with heliospheric distance—spectral indices converge toward f^-5/3 by 1 AU and the cascade rate decays away from the Sun. The authors test whether a much smaller astrophysical system, the planetary magnetosheath, exhibits analogous turbulence evolution and how upstream conditions control it.
AI.method: Analysis of 15 inbound magnetosheath crossings from the 2023 MMS unbiased magnetosheath campaign, tracking spectral index and cascade rate evolution with distance from the bow shock. WIND solar wind monitoring characterized upstream conditions, and incompressible Hall-MHD scaling-law estimates were used for cascade rates.
AI.result: Cascade rate increases by 2–3 orders of magnitude upon crossing the bow shock. Within the magnetosheath, turbulence develops with increasing bow-shock distance similarly to solar wind observations. Hall-MHD estimates show a clear power-law decay of cascade rate, most pronounced for upstream slow-wind cases.
AI.conclusion: The magnetosheath reproduces solar-wind-like turbulence evolution despite its small size, and the energy injection pathway (linked to upstream solar wind state) governs the spatial decay of the turbulent cascade.

title: Stellar Bars Reshape the Spatial Distribution of UV-bright Clumps in Nearby Galaxies
comment: 20 pages, 16 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Stellar bars redistribute gas and angular momentum in disk galaxies, but whether they mainly change the amount or the spatial organization of recent star formation remains uncertain. We use archival HST/WFC3 F275W imaging to study 70 barred galaxies and 95 unbarred control galaxies matched in stellar mass, optical color, redshift, and F275W background noise. A uniform dendrogram-based procedure identifies 95,486 UV-bright star-forming clumps. We compare their radial and azimuthal distributions, central F275W emission, and luminosity and size distribution functions. Relative to their controls, barred galaxies show a deficit of clumps at intermediate radii broadly corresponding to the bar region, followed by a local recovery near the bar ends. Their clumps are also preferentially concentrated along the bar major axis. These spatial differences are stronger in high-mass galaxies. Normalized bar length is more closely associated with the radial redistribution and central F275W concentration than bar ellipticity, although its relation to the azimuthal distribution is less uniform. When galactocentric radius is normalized by bar length, the recovery occurs near $R/R_{\rm bar}\sim1$, indicating that the bar sets a characteristic scale for the redistribution. Despite these spatial differences, barred and control galaxies have broadly similar clump luminosity and size distribution functions. Our results suggest that stellar bars mainly reorganize where recent star formation occurs, rather than substantially altering the observed luminosities and sizes of individual UV clumps, and that this effect depends on galaxy mass and bar extent.

AI.tldr: Using archival HST/WFC3 F275W imaging of 70 barred galaxies and 95 matched unbarred controls, this study finds that stellar bars primarily reorganize the spatial distribution of UV-bright star-forming clumps (depletion at bar-region radii, recovery near the bar ends, alignment along the bar major axis), while leaving clump luminosity and size distribution functions largely unchanged.
AI.motivation: It remains uncertain whether stellar bars mainly change the amount of recent star formation or its spatial organization within disk galaxies, despite bars being known to redistribute gas and angular momentum.
AI.method: Archival HST/WFC3 F275W imaging of 70 barred galaxies and 95 unbarred controls matched in stellar mass, optical color, redshift, and F275W background noise; a uniform dendrogram-based clump-finding procedure identifies 95,486 UV-bright star-forming clumps; comparison of radial and azimuthal clump distributions, central F275W emission, and luminosity/size distribution functions; analysis split by galaxy mass, bar length, and bar ellipticity, with radius normalized by bar length.
AI.result: Barred galaxies show a deficit of clumps at intermediate radii broadly coincident with the bar region, a local recovery near the bar ends (near R/R_bar ~ 1), and preferential concentration of clumps along the bar major axis; these differences are stronger in high-mass galaxies and relate more closely to normalized bar length than to bar ellipticity for radial redistribution and central F275W concentration, though the azimuthal dependence is less uniform; clump luminosity and size distribution functions are broadly similar between barred and control samples.
AI.conclusion: Stellar bars mainly reorganize where recent star formation occurs rather than substantially altering the observed luminosities and sizes of individual UV clumps, and this effect depends on galaxy mass and bar extent, with the bar setting a characteristic scale (R/R_bar ~ 1) for the redistribution.

title: The Unusual X-ray Spectrum of R Mon
comment: 18 pages, 2 tables, 4 figures
summary: The optically obscured young star R Mon illuminates Hubble's Variable Nebula and has historically been classified as an intermediate mass pre-main sequence Herbig Be star. We present Chandra observations of R Mon revealing a hard X-ray source viewed through high absorption from circumstellar gas known to be present from previous CO observations. The X-ray spectrum is characterized by line emission from the He-like Fe K complex (6.7 keV) tracing very hot plasma and fluorescent Fe emission (6.4 keV) from cold gas near the star that is irradiated by hard X-rays. Low-level variability on a timescale of less than one day is detected, but no large impulsive flares. The hot plasma and variability cannot be explained by shock models and magnetically confined plasma is inferred. The hard X-ray spectrum of R Mon does not resemble the soft spectra of prototypical Herbig stars but is remarkably similar to some class I protostars such as NGC 2071-IRS 1. As judged by its X-ray and infrared properties, we conclude that R Mon is a class I protostar and thus provides a rare snapshot of an emergent intermediate mass star enveloped in X-ray irradiated gas and dust.

AI.tldr: Chandra observations show R Mon, previously classified as a Herbig Be star, has a hard, heavily absorbed X-ray spectrum with hot magnetically confined plasma, indicating it is actually a class I protostar.
AI.motivation: R Mon has historically been classified as an intermediate-mass pre-main-sequence Herbig Be star, but its true evolutionary status and X-ray properties were unclear. The authors aim to characterize its X-ray emission and reassess its classification.
AI.method: Chandra X-ray observations of R Mon, spectral analysis of the He-like Fe K complex (6.7 keV) and fluorescent Fe (6.4 keV) emission, and variability analysis, complemented by comparison with Herbig stars and class I protostars and cross-reference with prior CO observations.
AI.result: A hard X-ray source seen through high circumstellar absorption, with hot plasma traced by 6.7 keV Fe K line emission, fluorescent 6.4 keV Fe from irradiated cold gas, low-level variability on sub-day timescales, and no large impulsive flares. The spectrum is unlike prototypical Herbig stars but closely resembles class I protostars such as NGC 2071-IRS 1.
AI.conclusion: Shock models cannot explain the hot plasma and variability, implying magnetically confined plasma. Based on X-ray and infrared properties, R Mon is reclassified as a class I protostar, offering a rare snapshot of an emergent intermediate-mass star enveloped in X-ray irradiated gas and dust.

title: Kinematic Map of the Galactic Bulge Using HST Proper Motions
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 1 table; submitted to MNRAS
summary: Constraining the Galactic bulge's non-axisymmetric dynamics requires proper motions in deep fields across many sightlines, yet crowding and extinction limit such measurements. Using multi-epoch observations of 27 fields in the southern Galactic bulge (-6$^\circ$ < l < 4$^\circ$, -5$^\circ$ < b < -1$^\circ$) from the ultraviolet-visible (UVIS) channel of Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) with time baselines of 3 to 13 years, and combining them with the absolute proper motion reference frame provided by Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3), we measure absolute proper motions for ~ 400,000 stars. Colour-magnitude diagrams are used to separate bulge stars from foreground disc stars, identify red clump stars and correct for interstellar extinction and reddening. Statistical analysis shows that the mean proper motion in Galactic latitude is consistent with that of the central supermassive black hole Sgr A*, while the mean proper motion in Galactic longitude is affected by disc stars but agrees with Sgr A* after extrapolation to the Galactic plane. Proper motion dispersions increase towards the Galactic centre and are asymmetric across Galactic longitude, with a steeper gradient for l < 0$^\circ$, revealing the bulge's non-axisymmetric bar structure. The velocity distribution shows clear anisotropy ($σ_l$/$σ_b$ = 1.131 $\pm$ 0.005). The normalised covariance is negative in the l > 0$^\circ$ region (~ -0.085) and close to zero in the l < 0$^\circ$ region. The proper motion distributions are non-Gaussian in both Galactic longitude and latitude, mainly due to contamination by foreground disc stars.

AI.tldr: Using 27 HST/WFC3 UVIS deep fields with 3–13 yr baselines anchored to Gaia DR3, the authors measure absolute proper motions for ~400,000 southern Galactic bulge stars, revealing anisotropy, asymmetric dispersions, and a bar-driven non-axisymmetric velocity structure.
AI.motivation: Constraining the Galactic bulge's non-axisymmetric dynamics (bar structure) requires deep, multi-sightline proper motions, but crowding and extinction hamper such measurements, especially in the highly obscured southern bulge.
AI.method: Multi-epoch HST/WFC3 UVIS observations of 27 fields (-6°<l<4°, -5°<b<-1°) with 3–13 yr baselines, tied to the Gaia DR3 absolute reference frame; colour-magnitude diagrams separate bulge from foreground disc stars, identify red clump stars, and correct extinction/reddening; statistical analysis of the proper motion distribution.
AI.result: Absolute proper motions for ~400,000 stars. Mean proper motion in Galactic latitude matches Sgr A*; mean in Galactic longitude is disc-contaminated but agrees with Sgr A* after extrapolation to the plane. Dispersions increase toward the Galactic centre and are asymmetric in l (steeper gradient for l<0°). Clear anisotropy (σ_l/σ_b = 1.131±0.005); normalised covariance is negative for l>0° (~-0.085) and ~zero for l<0°. Distributions are non-Gaussian in both coordinates, largely from foreground disc contamination.
AI.conclusion: The measured kinematics confirm the bulge's non-axisymmetric bar structure, quantify velocity anisotropy and covariance asymmetry, and validate the combination of HST depths with Gaia DR3 astrometry for bulge proper-motion studies.

title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths I: Energy Dissipation
comment: Revised version resubmitted to ApJ; 23 pages, 5 figures. includes supplementary material at the end of the file
summary: In this work, we study the turbulent origin of ion-scale Current Sheets (CSs) and the dissipation of energy via magnetic reconnection. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ ion data from Solar Orbiter, collected between July 2020 and September 2022. We apply an automatic detection algorithm that finds current sheets (CSs) of thickness (length in the normal direction, $λ$) near the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), and classifies them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. We compile a catalog of 974 CSs of thickness in the range of few to 90 ion inertial lengths, of which 53 contain an ion reconnection jet. We estimate that Solar Orbiter spends $\sim 1 \%$ of the dwell time inside a CS of few to 90 $δ_i$ thickness, and 0.06\% inside a reconnecting CS of the same thickness range. By comparing these results with previous studies we estimate that the abundance of CSs and of Reconnecting CSs evolves with heliocentric distance ($r$) as $r^{-0.9}$ and $r^{-1.5}$, respectively. We estimate that magnetic reconnection dissipates $ε_{rec}\sim 30 \hspace{5pt} \text{J} \text{kg}^{-1} \text{s}^{-1},$ in the $\sim 1 - 40$ $δ_i$ scale-range, by assessing the amount of plasma that interacts with a reconnection exhaust. We show how the dissipation of turbulence energy cascade by magnetic reconnection at scales smaller than 90 $δ_i$ is more effective closer to the Sun, and decays as $r^{-3.6}$. The current density of Alfvénic CSs thicker than the ion inertial length presents scale invariance, obeying $J_0/J_A=0.9(λ/2δ_i)^{-0.71}$, suggesting that CSs generated locally from solar wind turbulence.

AI.tldr: Using 103 hours of Solar Orbiter ion data, the authors build a catalog of 974 ion-scale current sheets, analyze their turbulent origin and reconnection-driven dissipation, and derive how current sheet abundance and energy dissipation scale with heliocentric distance.
AI.motivation: The origin of ion-scale current sheets from turbulence and their role in dissipating energy via magnetic reconnection in the solar wind remain unclear; a statistical, in-situ survey can quantify how common such sheets and reconnecting events are and how these quantities evolve with distance from the Sun.
AI.method: Analysis of 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data (July 2020–September 2022). An automatic detection algorithm identifies current sheets with thickness near the ion inertial length δ_i and classifies them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. The authors estimate dissipation by assessing the plasma volume interacting with reconnection exhausts and compare with prior studies to infer radial scaling.
AI.result: A catalog of 974 current sheets with thicknesses from a few to 90 δ_i, 53 containing ion reconnection jets. Solar Orbiter spends ~1% of dwell time inside a CS of few–90 δ_i thickness and 0.06% inside a reconnecting CS. CS abundance scales as r^-0.9 and reconnecting CS abundance as r^-1.5. Reconnection dissipates ε_rec ~ 30 J kg^-1 s^-1 in the ~1–40 δ_i range, decaying as r^-3.6. Alfvénic CSs thicker than δ_i show scale invariance, with J_0/J_A = 0.9(λ/2δ_i)^-0.71.
AI.conclusion: Turbulent dissipation via magnetic reconnection at scales below 90 δ_i is more effective closer to the Sun and weakens with heliocentric distance. The observed scale-invariant current density of Alfvénic sheets suggests these current sheets are generated locally by solar wind turbulence.

title: Resolving the Complex Line-Locking Structure in Quasar J004613+010425 with VLT/X-shooter Spectroscopy
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Line-locking (LL) signatures in quasar absorption-line systems provide direct observational evidence for radiatively driven outflows. We present a detailed investigation of LL phenomena in the quasar SDSS J004613.54+010425.7 ($z_{\rm em} = 2.150$) using medium-resolution VLT/X-shooter spectra, as part of the TOLL project. Compared with previous studies based on Sloan Digital Sky Survey spectroscopy, the X-shooter data resolve the absorption complex into twelve narrow absorption line (NAL) components spanning $\sim$$2700$ km/s in the C IV, N V, Si IV, and Ly$α$ transitions, a factor of $\sim$2.4 more components than identified from lower resolution spectra. We detect fourteen distinct LL pairs across three ionic species, forming one of the largest line-locking webs known to date: three Si IV pairs connecting components (2, 10), (4, 11), and (5, 12); six N V pairs organized into four groups; and five C IV pairs organized into three groups. Monte Carlo simulations show that the probability of this twelve-component LL web arising by chance is $< 10^{-5}$. Photoionization modeling with Cloudy yields ionization parameters of $\log U \approx -2.4$ to $-0.6$ and total hydrogen column densities of $\log N({\rm H}) \approx 18.4$-$20.6$ for the twelve components. A comparison of the properties of shadowed and shadowing clouds shows that ion column densities and ionization parameters typically agree within a factor of $\sim$3, broadly supporting the standard radiative acceleration picture, although several outliers suggest that multi-ion locking and cloud-cloud interactions may also regulate LL stability. These results demonstrate that medium- and high-resolution spectroscopy is essential for resolving the full complexity of line-locked quasar outflows.

AI.tldr: VLT/X-shooter spectroscopy of quasar SDSS J004613.54+010425.7 resolves a twelve-component C IV/N V/Si IV absorption complex forming one of the largest line-locking webs known, with chance probability below 10^-5, and Cloudy modeling broadly supports the standard radiative-acceleration picture.
AI.motivation: Line-locking signatures in quasar absorption systems provide direct evidence for radiatively driven outflows. Prior work relied on lower-resolution SDSS spectra that blended components and could not capture the full structure of line-locked systems, so the true complexity of these outflows remained unresolved.
AI.method: Medium-resolution VLT/X-shooter spectra (TOLL project) of SDSS J004613.54+010425.7 (z_em = 2.150) were used to decompose the absorption complex into twelve narrow absorption lines across C IV, N V, Si IV, and Ly-alpha. Line-locking pairs were identified across three ionic species, chance-coincidence assessed via Monte Carlo simulations, and physical conditions derived from Cloudy photoionization modeling, including a comparison of shadowing versus shadowed clouds.
AI.result: The complex resolves into twelve NAL components spanning ~2700 km/s, ~2.4 times more than in SDSS spectra. Fourteen distinct LL pairs are detected: three Si IV pairs ((2,10), (4,11), (5,12)), six N V pairs in four groups, and five C IV pairs in three groups. Monte Carlo simulations give a chance probability < 10^-5. Cloudy yields log U ~ -2.4 to -0.6 and log N(H) ~ 18.4-20.6; shadowed and shadowing clouds agree in column density and ionization parameter within a factor of ~3, with outliers suggesting multi-ion locking and cloud-cloud interactions.
AI.conclusion: The twelve-component line-locking web is highly unlikely to be coincidental and is broadly consistent with standard radiative acceleration, though multi-ion locking and cloud-cloud interactions may also regulate LL stability. Medium- and high-resolution spectroscopy is essential to resolve the full complexity of line-locked quasar outflows.

title: As a matter of reconstruction -- varying the magnetic Prandtl number in implicit large eddy simulations
comment: To be submitted, comments welcome!
summary: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} \not\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

AI.tldr: Varying the order of reconstruction schemes for hydrodynamic versus magnetic variables in a finite-volume ILES changes the effective magnetic Prandtl number, achieving over a 20-fold variation without explicit dissipation.
AI.motivation: Astrophysical plasmas span many orders of magnitude in magnetic Prandtl number (Pm = viscosity/magnetic diffusivity), which governs how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In DNS, viscosity and magnetic diffusivity are set independently, but in ILES they are fixed by the numerical scheme. The authors test whether Pm can be controlled in a finite-volume ILES.
AI.method: They simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous MHD turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. They apply different reconstruction orders to hydro and magnetic variables and measure effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales.
AI.result: Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective Pm (and vice versa). A mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone yields a ≳20× change in Pm. DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES results.
AI.conclusion: Mixed reconstruction offers a simple and efficient way to explore Pm ≠ 1 in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

title: OASIS I: Spectroscopy of Mini-Quenched and Lulling Galaxies Constrains the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
comment: 25 pages, 20 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to A&A. Paper I of the OASIS series; companion Papers II and III submitted simultaneously
summary: JWST has revealed that star formation in early galaxies is bursty, including episodes of violent suppression, so-called mini-quenching. But these were largely serendipitous discoveries in samples of UV-bright, emission-line-dominated galaxies, so that the quiet side of the burst cycle has remained poorly explored. With the JWST Cycle 3 program OASIS (GO 5997), we searched for such galaxies deliberately, using deep 28-hour NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy across the full burst cycle at z>4. We identify three mini-quenched galaxies with log(M*/Msun) = 8.3-8.9 and no detectable Balmer emission, at least 1.2-1.7 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS), five lulling galaxies with weak Balmer emission above the quenching threshold, and 17 nearly-main-sequence galaxies just below the SFMS. Finding them required spectroscopy: seven of our ten photometric candidates for suppressed (mini-quenched and lulling) galaxies turned out to be nearly-MS or above the SFMS, and photometric fits overestimate their current star-formation rates and cannot distinguish lulling from mini-quenched ones. The suppressed galaxies are common: five of the eight come from tiers not selected on star-formation state, where they make up 29% of the galaxies at z = 4-5.5 and log(M*/Msun) = 8-9.5, a number density of ~1.6x10^-3 Mpc^-3 dex^-1. Simulations predict them to be an order of magnitude rarer at these masses and to occur mainly at lower masses. The suppressed galaxies are also old: Balmer-break strength and stellar age both increase as galaxies fall further below the SFMS, with light-weighted ages of 5 Myr for galaxies above it, ~30 Myr for the lulling galaxies and above 100 Myr for the mini-quenched ones. They show little stellar reddening (E(B-V) < 0.2), consistent with depleted gas reservoirs. Suppressed phases at z>4 are therefore neither rare nor brief, but a common and lasting part of early galaxy growth.

AI.tldr: JWST OASIS spectroscopy deliberately searches for mini-quenched galaxies at z>4 and finds that suppressed star formation is common, long-lasting, and poorly captured by photometry.
AI.motivation: Bursty star formation with mini-quenching episodes in early galaxies has so far only been found serendipitously in UV-bright, emission-line-dominated samples, leaving the "quiet" side of the burst cycle largely unexplored. The authors aim to characterize suppressed (mini-quenched and lulling) galaxies systematically and deliberately.
AI.method: JWST Cycle 3 program OASIS (GO 5997) using deep 28-hour NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy across the full burst cycle at z>4, including tiers not selected on star-formation state. Galaxies are classified by Balmer emission, position relative to the SFMS, Balmer-break strength, and light-weighted stellar ages.
AI.result: Identified 3 mini-quenched galaxies (log M* = 8.3-8.9, no detectable Balmer emission, 1.2-1.7 dex below the SFMS), 5 lulling galaxies (weak Balmer emission above the quenching threshold), and 17 nearly-MS galaxies. Seven of ten photometric suppressed candidates were actually near or above the SFMS, showing photometry overestimates SFRs and cannot distinguish lulling from mini-quenching. Suppressed galaxies make up 29% of galaxies at z=4-5.5 with log M* = 8-9.5 (n ~ 1.6x10^-3 Mpc^-3 dex^-1), an order of magnitude more common and at higher masses than simulations predict. Ages increase with depth below the SFMS (~5 Myr above, ~30 Myr lulling, >100 Myr mini-quenched) with little reddening (E(B-V)<0.2).
AI.conclusion: Suppressed phases at z>4 are neither rare nor brief but a common and lasting part of early galaxy growth, requiring spectroscopy to identify reliably and indicating depleted gas reservoirs.

title: OASIS II: The Ionized Gas Traces Feedback-Driven Declines into the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Submitted to A&A. Paper II of the OASIS series; companion Papers I and III submitted simultaneously
summary: Models of bursty star formation in low-mass (10^8-10^9.5 Msun) galaxies at z>4 differ most in the suppressed phases: what drives the decline, how fast star formation falls, and how long it stays low. OASIS Paper I showed that such quiet galaxies are common and old; here we measure how they got there and how their ionized gas responds. We compare Balmer-line star-formation rates (SFRs) with 100-Myr averages from the stellar continuum, in NIRSpec/PRISM spectra of 54 OASIS galaxies at z>4, including three mini-quenched galaxies below the quenching threshold and five lulling galaxies at least 0.6 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) but still star-forming. Galaxies above the SFMS rise and fade equally often, whereas those below it are mostly fading: the lulling galaxies formed little more than a tenth of their mass in the last 100 Myr, and their decline began tens to ~100 Myr before observation. Suppressed phases thus last of order 100 Myr, as long as or longer than in most simulations, whereas recovery is much faster: few galaxies below the SFMS are rising. The ionized gas tracks these changes in star formation. [OIII]/[OII] falls from galaxies above the SFMS to the lulling ones, even at fixed mass and after dust correction, and follows the recent change in SFR (SFR_10/SFR_100) more closely than the position relative to the SFMS: two rising galaxies below the SFMS are highly ionized. This is expected if fewer and softer ionizing photons than in strongly star-forming galaxies meet gas depleted by earlier star formation. Lulling galaxies show ISM conditions distinct from those of strongly star-forming galaxies. The declines are faster than passive gas exhaustion predicts, favoring feedback that expels the gas or keeps it from forming stars. Quiet phases are thus long, feedback-driven episodes, and the ionized gas traces where a galaxy is in its burst cycle.

AI.tldr: The paper measures the dynamics of bursty star formation in z>4 low-mass galaxies, finding that quiet (suppressed) phases last ~100 Myr and are feedback-driven, and that gas excitation ([OIII]/[OII]) tracks the recent change in SFR rather than the position relative to the SFMS.
AI.motivation: Models of bursty star formation in low-mass galaxies at z>4 disagree most about the suppressed phases—what drives the decline, how fast SFR falls, and how long it stays low. OASIS Paper I showed quiet galaxies are common and old; this work probes the mechanism and timescales.
AI.method: Compares Balmer-line SFRs with 100-Myr stellar-continuum averages in NIRSpec/PRISM spectra of 54 OASIS galaxies at z>4, including 3 mini-quenched galaxies below the quenching threshold and 5 "lulling" galaxies at least 0.6 dex below the SFMS but still star-forming.
AI.result: Galaxies above the SFMS rise and fade equally often, while those below are mostly fading: lulling galaxies formed barely a tenth of their mass in the last 100 Myr, and declines began tens to ~100 Myr before observation. [OIII]/[OII] falls from above-SFMS to lulling galaxies (even at fixed mass, after dust correction) and tracks SFR_10/SFR_100 more closely than SFMS offset; two rising below-SFMS galaxies are highly ionized.
AI.conclusion: Suppressed phases last of order ~100 Myr—as long as or longer than most simulations—while recovery is much faster (few below-SFMS galaxies are rising). Declines are faster than passive gas exhaustion predicts, favoring feedback that expels or suppresses gas. Quiet phases are long, feedback-driven episodes, and ionized gas traces the burst cycle phase.

title: OASIS III: Bursty star formation drives observed galaxy sizes at $z\geq4$
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 1 table. Submitted to A&A
